title: 2 Corinthians

stories.title: 🕊️ 2 Corinthians 1
summaryBullets: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, To the church of God in Corinth, together with all the saints throughout Achaia: (1:1).
Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. (1:2).
Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of compassion and the God of all comfort, (1:3).
who comforts us in all our troubles, so that we can comfort those in any trouble with the comfort we ourselves have received from God. (1:4).
For just as the sufferings of Christ overflow to us, so also through Christ our comfort overflows. (1:5).
If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation; if we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which accomplishes in you patient endurance of the same sufferings we experience. (1:6).
And our hope for you is sure, because we know that just as you share in our sufferings, so also you will share in our comfort. (1:7).
We do not want you to be unaware, brothers, of the hardships we encountered in the province of Asia. We were under a burden far beyond our ability to endure, so that we despaired even of life. (1:8).
Indeed, we felt we were under the sentence of death, in order that we would not trust in ourselves, but in God, who raises the dead. (1:9).
He has delivered us from such a deadly peril, and He will deliver us. In Him we have placed our hope that He will yet again deliver us, (1:10).
as you help us by your prayers. Then many will give thanks on our behalf for the favor shown us in answer to their prayers. (1:11).

For this is our boast: Our conscience testifies that we have conducted ourselves in the world, and especially in relation to you, in the holiness and sincerity that are from God — not in worldly wisdom, but in the grace of God. (1:12).
For we do not write you anything that is beyond your ability to read and understand. And I hope that you will understand us completely, (1:13).
as you have already understood us in part, that you may boast of us just as we will boast of you in the day of our Lord Jesus. (1:14).
Confident of this, I planned to visit you first, so that you might receive a double blessing. (1:15).
I wanted to visit you on my way to Macedonia, and to return to you from Macedonia, and then to have you help me on my way to Judea. (1:16).
When I planned this, did I do it carelessly? Or do I make my plans by human standards, so as to say “Yes, yes” and also “No, no”? (1:17).
But as surely as God is faithful, our message to you is not “Yes” and “No.” (1:18).
For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was proclaimed among you by me and Silvanus and Timothy, was not “Yes” and “No,” but in Him it has always been “Yes.” (1:19).
For all the promises of God are “Yes” in Christ. And so through Him, our “Amen” is spoken to the glory of God. (1:20).
Now it is God who establishes both us and you in Christ. He anointed us, (1:21).
placed His seal on us, and put His Spirit in our hearts as a pledge of what is to come. (1:22).
I call God as my witness that it was in order to spare you that I did not return to Corinth. (1:23).
Not that we lord it over your faith, but we are fellow workers with you for your joy, because it is by faith that you stand firm. (1:24).
crossRefs: Isaiah 51:12: I am he who comforts you.
Romans 8:18: Sufferings not worth comparing with glory.
Acts 19:23-29: Paul’s affliction in Asia (Ephesus riot).
Psalm 34:19: Many are the afflictions of the righteous.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נֶחָמָה (neḥāmāh), Greek: παράκλησις (paráklēsis, NT), Aramaic: בּוּיַא (būyā)
translationNotes.note: Means encouragement, strengthening, consolation; repeated as theme in vv. 3-7.

A Hebrew word carried into Greek untranslated, from a root meaning firm or reliable. It was the assembly's spoken agreement to words read aloud: the people answer 'Amen, Amen' with lifted hands in Nehemiah 8:6, and each of the twelve curses in Deuteronomy 27:15-26 ends with all the people saying it. That is the setting of 1:20, where the promises are Yes in Christ and the church speaks the Amen through him.

Not the continent. Asia was a Roman province covering the western end of Asia Minor, in what is now Turkey, governed by a proconsul with Ephesus as its leading city. The affliction that came on Paul 'in Asia' (1:8) happened in that province, and Acts 19:23-41 records the riot at Ephesus.

The same man Acts calls Silas. Silvanus is the Latin form of the name and Silas the shorter Greek form, and the two writers are consistent: Acts always says Silas, Paul always says Silvanus (1:19, 1 Thessalonians 1:1, 2 Thessalonians 1:1). Peter names him as the man who carried his letter (1 Peter 5:12).

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul blesses the God of all comfort, who comforts the afflicted so they can comfort others, and recounts despairing even of life in Asia so that he would trust God who raises the dead; he defends his changed travel plans as sincere, for in Christ all God’s promises are Yes, God has sealed believers and given the Spirit as a pledge, and he stayed away from Corinth to spare them.

stories.title: 📜 2 Corinthians 2
summaryBullets: So I made up my mind not to make another painful visit to you. (2:1).
For if I grieve you, who is left to cheer me but those whom I have grieved? (2:2).
I wrote as I did so that on my arrival I would not be grieved by those who ought to make me rejoice. I had confidence in all of you, that you would share my joy. (2:3).
For through many tears I wrote you out of great distress and anguish of heart, not to grieve you but to let you know how much I love you. (2:4).
Now if anyone has caused grief, he has not grieved me but all of you — to some degree, not to overstate it. (2:5).
The punishment imposed on him by the majority is sufficient for him. (2:6).
So instead, you ought to forgive and comfort him, so that he will not be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow. (2:7).
Therefore I urge you to reaffirm your love for him. (2:8).
My purpose in writing you was to see if you would stand the test and be obedient in everything. (2:9).
If you forgive anyone, I also forgive him. And if I have forgiven anything, I have forgiven it in the presence of Christ for your sake, (2:10).
in order that Satan should not outwit us. For we are not unaware of his schemes. (2:11).
Now when I went to Troas to preach the gospel of Christ and a door stood open for me in the Lord, (2:12).
I had no peace in my spirit, because I did not find my brother Titus there. So I said goodbye to them and went on to Macedonia. (2:13).
But thanks be to God, who always leads us triumphantly as captives in Christ and through us spreads everywhere the fragrance of the knowledge of Him. (2:14).
For we are to God the sweet aroma of Christ among those who are being saved and those who are perishing. (2:15).
To the one we are an odor that brings death, to the other a fragrance that brings life. And who is qualified for such a task? (2:16).
For we are not like so many others, who peddle the word of God for profit. On the contrary, in Christ we speak before God with sincerity, as men sent from God. (2:17).
crossRefs: 1 Corinthians 5:1-5: Case of the immoral man.
Matthew 18:21-22: Forgive seventy times seven.
Ephesians 1:13: Sealed with the Spirit.
John 20:23: Authority to forgive.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כֵּן וְלֹא (kēn wəlōʾ, sense), Greek: ναί καὶ οὔ (naί kaὶ oὔ, NT), Aramaic: הן ולא (הן ולא)
translationNotes.note: Paul denies duplicity; stresses that in Christ all God’s promises are affirmed.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֵרָבוֹן (ʿērāvon), Greek: ἀρραβών (arrabṓn, NT), Aramaic: ערבון (ʿarāvōn)
translationNotes.note: Term for down payment or pledge; the Spirit given as first installment of God’s future promise.

The verb names a Roman triumph, the parade voted to a victorious general. He rode to the temple of Jupiter on the Capitol while incense burned along the route, and the prisoners taken in the war walked behind the chariot; the chief captive was commonly executed when the parade ended, as Vercingetorix was after five years in prison at Caesar's triumph in 46 BC. In 2:14-16 Paul puts himself in the procession rather than the chariot, and the smoke that rises is life to one side of the road and death to the other.

A kapelos was a small retail dealer, above all a wine seller, and the trade was proverbial for watering the stock. Plato used the same verb of men who hawk learning for a fee (Protagoras 313d). The charge in 2:17 is not that the rivals sell but that they adulterate.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul explains his change of travel plans, affirms sincerity, recalls his painful letter, and urges forgiveness for the repentant offender.

stories.title: 📜 2 Corinthians 3
summaryBullets: Are we beginning to commend ourselves again? Or do we need, like some people, letters of recommendation to you or from you? (3:1).
You yourselves are our letter, inscribed on our hearts, known and read by everyone. (3:2).
It is clear that you are a letter from Christ, the result of our ministry, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts. (3:3).
Such confidence before God is ours through Christ. (3:4).
Not that we are competent in ourselves to claim that anything comes from us, but our competence comes from God. (3:5).
And He has qualified us as ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life. (3:6).
Now if the ministry of death, which was engraved in letters on stone, came with such glory that the Israelites could not gaze at the face of Moses because of its fleeting glory, (3:7).
will not the ministry of the Spirit be even more glorious? (3:8).
For if the ministry of condemnation was glorious, how much more glorious is the ministry of righteousness! (3:9).
Indeed, what was once glorious has no glory now in comparison to the glory that surpasses it. (3:10).
For if what was fading away came with glory, how much greater is the glory of that which endures! (3:11).
Therefore, since we have such a hope, we are very bold. (3:12).
We are not like Moses, who would put a veil over his face to keep the Israelites from gazing at the end of what was fading away. (3:13).
But their minds were closed. For to this day the same veil remains at the reading of the old covenant. It has not been lifted, because only in Christ can it be removed. (3:14).
And even to this day when Moses is read, a veil covers their hearts. (3:15).
But whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away. (3:16).
Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom. (3:17).
And we, who with unveiled faces all reflect the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into His image with intensifying glory, which comes from the Lord, who is the Spirit. (3:18).
crossRefs: Exodus 34:29-35: Moses’ face shining with glory.
Jeremiah 31:31-33: New covenant on hearts.
Romans 7:6: Serve in new way of the Spirit.
Galatians 5:1: Freedom in Christ.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אוֹת הוֹרֵג (ʾwōt hwōrēg, sense), Greek: τὸ γράμμα ἀποκτέννει (tὸ grάmma ἀpoktέnnei, NT), Aramaic: כתבא קטיל (כתבא קטיל)
translationNotes.note: Refers to written law without Spirit; contrasts external command with inner transformation.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַסְוֶה (masəweh), Greek: κάλυμμα (kάlymma, NT), Aramaic: מסותא (מסותא)
translationNotes.note: Cloth covering Moses’ shining face; used as image of spiritual dullness removed in Christ.

Ordinary ancient business. A traveler carried a short letter from a known patron asking the recipient to house him, feed him and stand behind his credit, and many such letters survive on papyrus from Egypt. Paul writes one for Phoebe in Romans 16:1-2 and the believers at Ephesus write ahead for Apollos in Acts 18:27; in 3:1-3 he says the Corinthians themselves are his letter.

Reading was public and out loud, not private and silent. James tells the council that Moses has been read in the synagogues every Sabbath from ancient generations (Acts 15:21), and Luke 4:16-20 gives the mechanics: the reader stands, is handed the scroll, reads, rolls it up, hands it back, and sits down to speak. That weekly reading is the scene behind 3:14-15.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul contrasts the old covenant on stone with the Spirit’s new covenant, describing believers as transformed by God’s glory.

headings.text: The Glory of the New Covenant

stories.title: 🌿 2 Corinthians 4
summaryBullets: Therefore, since God in His mercy has given us this ministry, we do not lose heart. (4:1).

Instead, we have renounced secret and shameful ways. We do not practice deceit, nor do we distort the word of God. On the contrary, by open proclamation of the truth, we commend ourselves to every man’s conscience in the sight of God. (4:2).
And even if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing. (4:3).
The god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, so they cannot see the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God. (4:4).
For we do not proclaim ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake. (4:5).
For God, who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” made His light shine in our hearts to give us the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ. (4:6).
Now we have this treasure in jars of clay to show that this surpassingly great power is from God and not from us. (4:7).
We are hard pressed on all sides, but not crushed; perplexed, but not in despair; (4:8).
persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed. (4:9).
We always carry around in our body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in our body. (4:10).
For we who are alive are always consigned to death for Jesus’ sake, so that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in our mortal body. (4:11).
So then, death is at work in us, but life is at work in you. (4:12).
And in keeping with what is written, “I believed, therefore I have spoken,” we who have the same spirit of faith also believe and therefore speak, (4:13).
knowing that the One who raised the Lord Jesus will also raise us with Jesus and present us with you in His presence. (4:14).
All this is for your benefit, so that the grace that is extending to more and more people may cause thanksgiving to overflow, to the glory of God. (4:15).
Therefore we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, yet our inner self is being renewed day by day. (4:16).
For our light and momentary affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory that is far beyond comparison. (4:17).
So we fix our eyes not on what is seen, but on what is unseen. For what is seen is temporary, but what is unseen is eternal. (4:18).
crossRefs: Genesis 1:3: Let there be light.
Job 33:28: Delivered from pit to see light.
Romans 8:18: Sufferings vs future glory.
Philippians 3:21: Transformation of our lowly body.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כְּלֵי חָרֶשׂ (kəlê ḥāres), Greek: ὀστράκινα σκεύη (ostrakina skeuē, NT), Aramaic: מנא דחרסא (manā d-ḥarsā)
translationNotes.note: Fragile pottery vessels; metaphor for human weakness carrying the gospel’s divine power (4:7).

The King James renders 4:4 'the god of this world', but the Greek word is aion, an age or stretch of time, not kosmos, the world as a place. Paul means the present era of history: the same word gives 'this present evil age' in Galatians 1:4 and 'do not be conformed to this age' in Romans 12:2.

The Hebrew word for glory, kavod, is built on the root for being heavy; the same root gives the ordinary word for a heavy load. The Greek translators rendered it doxa, which in normal Greek meant opinion or reputation, and English 'glory' inherited that side of it. In 4:17 Paul puts the two halves back together: an affliction that is light, weighed against an eternal baros, a weight, of glory.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ἐπίστευσα, διὸ ἐλάλησα (episteusa, dio elalesa)
translationNotes.note: Paul quotes Psalm 116:10 at 4:13, and he quotes it from the Greek Old Testament, where the verse stands at Psalm 115:1 because the Greek splits the psalm in two. The Greek reads 'I believed, therefore I spoke'; the Hebrew line runs differently and is usually given as 'I believed, even when I said, I am greatly afflicted.' Most Old Testament quotations in the New Testament follow the Greek version, which is why a quotation sometimes does not match the Old Testament page it came from.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul describes carrying Christ’s life in frail bodies, enduring affliction, and fixing eyes on eternal glory.

stories.title: 🌿 2 Corinthians 5
summaryBullets: For we know that if the earthly tent we live in is dismantled, we have a building from God, an eternal house in heaven, not built by human hands. (5:1).
For in this tent we groan, longing to be clothed with our heavenly dwelling, (5:2).
because when we are clothed, we will not be found naked. (5:3).
For while we are in this tent, we groan under our burdens, because we do not wish to be unclothed but clothed, so that our mortality may be swallowed up by life. (5:4).
And it is God who has prepared us for this very purpose and has given us the Spirit as a pledge of what is to come. (5:5).
Therefore we are always confident, although we know that while we are at home in the body, we are away from the Lord. (5:6).
For we walk by faith, not by sight. (5:7).
We are confident, then, and would prefer to be away from the body and at home with the Lord. (5:8).
So we aspire to please Him, whether we are at home in this body or away from it. (5:9).
For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, that each one may receive his due for the things done in the body, whether good or bad. (5:10).
Therefore, since we know what it means to fear the Lord, we try to persuade men. What we are is clear to God, and I hope it is clear to your conscience as well. (5:11).
We are not commending ourselves to you again. Instead, we are giving you an occasion to be proud of us, so that you can answer those who take pride in appearances rather than in the heart. (5:12).
If we are out of our mind, it is for God; if we are of sound mind, it is for you. (5:13).
For Christ’s love compels us, because we are convinced that One died for all, therefore all died. (5:14).
And He died for all, that those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for Him who died for them and was raised again. (5:15).
So from now on we regard no one according to the flesh. Although we once regarded Christ in this way, we do so no longer. (5:16).
Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away. Behold, the new has come! (5:17).
All this is from God, who reconciled us to Himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation: (5:18).
that God was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ, not counting men’s trespasses against them. And He has committed to us the message of reconciliation. (5:19).
Therefore we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were making His appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ: Be reconciled to God. (5:20).
God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God. (5:21).
crossRefs: Isaiah 53:4-6: The servant carries the griefs of others, and the LORD lays on him the iniquity of us all.
Romans 8:23: Those who have the firstfruits of the Spirit groan inwardly, waiting for the redemption of the body.
Romans 14:10-12: Every one of us will stand before the judgment seat of God and give an account of himself.
1 Corinthians 15:53-54: The perishable puts on the imperishable, and death is swallowed up in victory.
Galatians 6:15: Neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything; what counts is a new creation.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כִּסֵּא מִשְׁפָּט (kisēʾ mišəpāṭ, sense), Greek: βῆμα (bῆma, NT), Aramaic: בּימתא (בּימתא)
translationNotes.note: Raised platform for judicial decisions; image for Christ’s tribunal.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שָׁלוּחַ (šālwḥa, sense), Greek: πρεσβεύομεν (presbeύomen, NT), Aramaic: שליחיא (שליחיא)
translationNotes.note: Official envoys representing authority; Paul applies it to gospel ministry.

Paul worked at the tent trade in Corinth with Aquila and Priscilla, cutting and stitching cloth or leather panels (Acts 18:1-3). In 5:1-4 he uses the trade for the body: a tent that gets struck and folded away, set against a building from God not made with hands. The same word group names the tabernacle, the tent Israel carried through the wilderness.

The verb first meant to exchange one thing for another, including changing money into other coin, and from that to change enmity into friendship. It was ordinary language for ending a quarrel between two men or two cities. The word group appears five times in 5:18-20, and the accounting sense stays live: 5:19 says God was not reckoning their trespasses to their account.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul teaches that believers groan while trapped in their mortal bodies but possess the Holy Spirit as a guarantee of their eternal heavenly home; he urges them to live for Christ and serve as ambassadors of reconciliation, since Christ died for all and rose again.

stories.title: 🌿 2 Corinthians 6
summaryBullets: As God’s fellow workers, then, we urge you not to receive God’s grace in vain. (6:1).
For He says: “In the time of favor I heard you, and in the day of salvation I helped you.” Behold, now is the time of favor; now is the day of salvation! (6:2).
We put no obstacle in anyone’s way, so that no one can discredit our ministry. (6:3).
Rather, as servants of God we commend ourselves in every way: in great endurance; in troubles, hardships, and calamities; (6:4).
in beatings, imprisonments, and riots; in labor, sleepless nights, and hunger; (6:5).
in purity, knowledge, patience, and kindness; in the Holy Spirit and in sincere love; (6:6).
in truthful speech and in the power of God; with the weapons of righteousness in the right hand and in the left; (6:7).
through glory and dishonor, slander and praise; viewed as imposters, yet genuine; (6:8).
unknown, yet well-known; dying, and yet we live on; punished, yet not killed; (6:9).
sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; poor, yet making many rich; having nothing, and yet possessing everything. (6:10).
We have spoken freely to you, Corinthians. Our hearts are open wide. (6:11).
It is not our affection, but yours, that is restrained. (6:12).
As a fair exchange— I speak as to my children— open wide your hearts also. (6:13).
Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership can righteousness have with wickedness? Or what fellowship does light have with darkness? (6:14).
What harmony is there between Christ and Belial? Or what does a believer have in common with an unbeliever? (6:15).

What agreement can exist between the temple of God and idols? For we are the temple of the living God. As God has said: “I will dwell with them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be My people.” (6:16).
“Therefore come out from among them and be separate, says the Lord. Touch no unclean thing, and I will receive you.” (6:17).
And: “I will be a Father to you, and you will be My sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty.” (6:18).
crossRefs: Isaiah 49:8: In a time of favor I answered you, and in a day of salvation I helped you.
Leviticus 26:11-12: God promises to set his dwelling among them, walk among them, and be their God.
Ezekiel 37:26-27: My dwelling place will be with them; I will be their God and they will be my people.
Isaiah 52:11: Depart, touch no unclean thing, come out from her midst, you who carry the vessels of the LORD.
2 Samuel 7:14: I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כִּסֵּא מִשְׁפָּט (kisēʾ mišəpāṭ, sense), Greek: βῆμα (bῆma, NT), Aramaic: בּימתא (בּימתא)
translationNotes.note: Raised platform for judicial decisions; image for Christ’s tribunal.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שָׁלוּחַ (šālwḥa, sense), Greek: πρεσβεύομεν (presbeύomen, NT), Aramaic: שליחיא (שליחיא)
translationNotes.note: Official envoys representing authority; Paul applies it to gospel ministry.

Roman law did not use prison as a sentence. A convicted man was fined, flogged, exiled, sent to the mines or executed; the lockup held people awaiting trial or execution, so time in prison was custody, not the punishment itself. Prisoners were fed and clothed by their friends, which is why Paul thanks the Philippians for what they sent (Philippians 4:14-18) and why Onesiphorus hunting him down in Rome is worth recording (2 Timothy 1:16-17).

The Greek word means the inward organs, the heart, liver, lungs and kidneys, which is where the ancient world located strong feeling; the King James renders it 'bowels'. In 6:11-12 Paul says his own splanchna are open wide and theirs are cramped shut. English moves the seat of feeling up to the heart, so the physical force of the image drops out.

translationNotes.term: Weapons of the right hand and the left
translationNotes.original: Greek: ὅπλα δεξιῶν καὶ ἀριστερῶν (hopla dexion kai aristeron)
translationNotes.note: A soldier held his sword in the right hand and carried his shield on the left arm. Armed on both sides means equipped to attack and to defend at once, so the phrase in 6:7 is a fighting kit and not a figure for balance. Paul lays the whole set out piece by piece in Ephesians 6:14-17.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul urges the Corinthians not to waste God's grace and details his own sufferings and virtues as a servant of God, then appeals for them to reciprocate his affection and warns them against being bound with unbelievers since believers are God's temple.

stories.title: 📜 2 Corinthians 7
summaryBullets: Therefore, beloved, since we have these promises, let us cleanse ourselves from everything that defiles body and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God. (7:1).
Make room for us in your hearts. We have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one, we have exploited no one. (7:2).
I do not say this to condemn you. I have said before that you so occupy our hearts that we live and die together with you. (7:3).
Great is my confidence in you; great is my pride in you; I am filled with encouragement; in all our troubles my joy overflows. (7:4).
For when we arrived in Macedonia, our bodies had no rest, but we were pressed from every direction — conflicts on the outside, fears within. (7:5).
But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the arrival of Titus, (7:6).
and not only by his arrival, but also by the comfort he had received from you. He told us about your longing, your mourning, and your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced all the more. (7:7).
Even if I caused you sorrow by my letter, I do not regret it. Although I did regret it— for I see that my letter caused you sorrow, but only for a short time— (7:8).
yet now I rejoice, not because you were made sorrowful, but because your sorrow led you to repentance. For you felt the sorrow that God had intended, and so were not harmed in any way by us. (7:9).
Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret, but worldly sorrow brings death. (7:10).

Consider what this godly sorrow has produced in you: what earnestness, what eagerness to clear yourselves, what indignation, what alarm, what longing, what zeal, what vindication! In every way you have proved yourselves to be innocent in this matter. (7:11).

So even though I wrote to you, it was not on account of the one who did wrong or the one who was harmed, but rather that your earnestness on our behalf would be made clear to you in the sight of God. (7:12).
On account of this, we are encouraged. In addition to our own encouragement, we were even more delighted by the joy of Titus. For his spirit has been refreshed by all of you. (7:13).
Indeed, I was not embarrassed by anything I had boasted to him about you. But just as everything we said to you was true, so our boasting to Titus has proved to be true as well. (7:14).
And his affection for you is even greater when he remembers that you were all obedient as you welcomed him with fear and trembling. (7:15).
I rejoice that I can have complete confidence in you. (7:16).
crossRefs: 2 Corinthians 2:12-13: Paul finds no rest at Troas because Titus is not there, and crosses to Macedonia.
Matthew 27:3-5: Judas is seized with remorse, throws back the silver, and hangs himself.
Isaiah 57:15: God dwells in the high and holy place and with the contrite and lowly, to revive their heart.
Psalm 34:18: The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit.
Jeremiah 31:18-19: Ephraim, disciplined and ashamed, strikes his thigh and asks to be restored.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֹל שָׁוֶה (ʿol shavéh, sense), Greek: ἑτεροζυγοῦντες (heterozygoûntes, NT), Aramaic: טורין דשנין (ṭūrin d-shenin)
translationNotes.note: Farming image of mismatched animals under one yoke. Paul applies it to incompatible partnerships between believer and unbeliever (6:14-16).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּלִיַּעַל (beliyyaʿal), Greek: Βελιάρ (Beliár, NT), Aramaic: בליעל (belīʿal)
translationNotes.note: Term meaning worthlessness/lawlessness; used here as a name for Satan or personified evil (6:15).

English blurs two Greek words in 7:8-10. Metamelomai is being sorry about a thing afterward, a change of feeling, and it is what Paul says he no longer is about the painful letter. Metanoia is a change of mind that turns and goes the other way, and that is what he says their grief produced. Matthew 27:3 uses the first word of Judas and never the second.

There was no public mail for private letters. The imperial post Augustus organized carried government dispatches only, so an ordinary letter went by a traveler, a merchant, or a servant sent for the purpose, and an answer could take months. That is why Paul is pacing at Troas and in Macedonia waiting on Titus (2:12-13, 7:5-7): the letter and the news travelled at the speed of a man on a road.

stories.keyTakeaway: Since these promises stand, Paul urges cleansing from everything that defiles, perfecting holiness in the fear of God, and asks the Corinthians to make room in their hearts; comforted in Macedonia by Titus’s arrival and report, he rejoices that their godly sorrow produced repentance leading to salvation, shown in earnestness, zeal, and obedience that renewed his confidence.

stories.title: 🌿 2 Corinthians 8
summaryBullets: Now, brothers, we want you to know about the grace that God has given the churches of Macedonia. (8:1).
In the terrible ordeal they suffered, their abundant joy and deep poverty overflowed into rich generosity. (8:2).
For I testify that they gave according to their ability and even beyond it. Of their own accord, (8:3).
they earnestly pleaded with us for the privilege of sharing in this service to the saints. (8:4).
And not only did they do as we expected, but they gave themselves first to the Lord and then to us, through the will of God. (8:5).
So we urged Titus to help complete your act of grace, just as he had started it. (8:6).
But just as you excel in everything — in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in complete earnestness, and in the love we inspired in you — see that you also excel in this grace of giving. (8:7).
I am not giving a command, but I am testing the sincerity of your love through the earnestness of others. (8:8).
For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though He was rich, yet for your sake He became poor, so that you through His poverty might become rich. (8:9).
And this is my opinion about what is helpful for you in this matter: Last year you were the first not only to give, but even to have such a desire. (8:10).
Now finish the work, so that you may complete it with the same eager desire, according to your means. (8:11).
For if the eagerness is there, the gift is acceptable according to what one has, not according to what he does not have. (8:12).
It is not our intention that others may be relieved while you are burdened, but that there may be equality. (8:13).
At the present time, your surplus will meet their need, so that in turn their surplus will meet your need. This way there will be equality. (8:14).
As it is written: “He who gathered much had no excess, and he who gathered little had no shortfall.” (8:15).
But thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same devotion I have for you. (8:16).
For not only did he welcome our appeal, but he is eagerly coming to you of his own volition. (8:17).
Along with Titus we are sending the brother who is praised by all the churches for his work in the gospel. (8:18).
More than that, this brother was chosen by the churches to accompany us with the gracious offering we administer to honor the Lord Himself and to show our eagerness to help. (8:19).
We want to avoid any criticism of the way we administer this generous gift. (8:20).
For we are taking great care to do what is right, not only in the eyes of the Lord, but also in the eyes of men. (8:21).
And we are sending along with them our brother who has proven his earnestness to us many times and in many ways, and now even more so by his great confidence in you. (8:22).
As for Titus, he is my partner and fellow worker among you. As for our brothers, they are messengers of the churches, the glory of Christ. (8:23).
In full view of the churches, then, show these men the proof of your love and the reason for our boasting about you. (8:24).
crossRefs: Exodus 16:18: Gathering manna equally.
Philippians 4:15: Philippians shared in giving.
Acts 11:29: Disciples sent relief to Judea.
2 Corinthians 9:7: God loves a cheerful giver.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הִדָּלָה (hidālāh, sense), Greek: ἐπτώχευσεν (ἐptώcheusen, NT), Aramaic: אתדליל (אתדליל)
translationNotes.note: Refers to Christ giving up riches of divine glory to embrace poverty for human salvation.

Chapters 8 and 9 are about one specific fund: relief money gathered in the Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem. Paul had agreed to it with James, Peter and John (Galatians 2:10), gave Corinth instructions for weekly saving in 1 Corinthians 16:1-4, and carried it up in Romans 15:25-28. The word for it in 1 Corinthians 16:1, logeia, is not a literary term; Adolf Deissmann showed in 1908 that it is the word in Egyptian papyri for a collection or levy taken for religious purposes.

One Greek word runs through this chapter under four English renderings. In 8:1 it is the grace God gave the Macedonians, in 8:4 the privilege of sharing in the relief work, in 8:6-7 the act of giving itself, and in 8:16 thanks to God. Read 8:1-7 with one word in mind and the money and the kindness turn out to be called the same thing.

Paul refuses to travel alone with the fund. The churches elected a delegate to go with him (8:19), and 8:20-21 says why: so that no one can fault him over this large sum, since he aims at what is honorable before men as well as before the Lord. Jewish communities abroad took the same precaution with the temple tax, sending it under escort; Cicero's defence of Flaccus in 59 BC turns on gold collected for Jerusalem in the province of Asia.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul commends the Macedonians’ generosity, urges the Corinthians to complete their gift, and sends Titus with companions to ensure integrity.

stories.title: 🌿 2 Corinthians 9
summaryBullets: Now about the service to the saints, there is no need for me to write to you. (9:1).
For I know your eagerness to help, and I have been boasting to the Macedonians that since last year you in Achaia were prepared to give. And your zeal has stirred most of them to do likewise. (9:2).
But I am sending the brothers in order that our boasting about you in this matter should not prove empty, but that you will be prepared, just as I said. (9:3).
Otherwise, if any Macedonians come with me and find you unprepared, we — to say nothing of you — would be ashamed of having been so confident. (9:4).

So I thought it necessary to urge the brothers to visit you beforehand and make arrangements for the generous gift you had promised. This way, your gift will be prepared generously and not begrudgingly. (9:5).
Remember this: Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows generously will also reap generously. (9:6).
Each one should give what he has decided in his heart to give, not out of regret or compulsion. For God loves a cheerful giver. (9:7).
And God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that in all things, at all times, having all that you need, you will abound in every good work. (9:8).
As it is written: “He has scattered abroad His gifts to the poor; His righteousness endures forever.” (9:9).
Now He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your store of seed and will increase the harvest of your righteousness. (9:10).
You will be enriched in every way to be generous on every occasion, and through us your generosity will produce thanksgiving to God. (9:11).
For this ministry of service is not only supplying the needs of the saints but is also overflowing in many expressions of thanksgiving to God. (9:12).

Because of the proof this ministry provides, the saints will glorify God for your obedient confession of the gospel of Christ, and for the generosity of your contribution to them and to all the others. (9:13).
And their prayers for you will express their affection for you, because of the surpassing grace God has given you. (9:14).
Thanks be to God for His indescribable gift! (9:15).
crossRefs: Proverbs 11:25: Whoever refreshes will be refreshed.
Luke 6:38: Give, and it will be given to you.
Psalm 112:9: He has distributed freely to the poor.
Galatians 6:7: A man reaps what he sows.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נָדִיב לֵב (nādiyb lēb), Greek: ἱλαρὸν δότην (ἱlarὸn dόtēn, NT), Aramaic: נדיבא דלבא (נדיבא דלבא)
translationNotes.note: Phrase means glad-hearted generosity; not coerced giving.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַתָּנָה נִפְלָאָה (matānāh nipəlāʾāh, sense), Greek: ἀνεκδιήγητος δωρεά (ἀnekdiήgētos dōreά, NT), Aramaic: מתנתא דלא מתפרשא (מתנתא דלא מתפרשא)
translationNotes.note: Unique expression for God’s supreme gift, often understood as Christ or grace itself.

In a Greek city a leitourgia was a public duty a rich citizen paid for out of his own pocket: fitting out a warship, training a chorus for the festival, funding a grain distribution. It was an honor and a bill at the same time. Paul gives the relief fund that name in 9:12, so the collection is being described as civic service performed for the saints, which the English word 'ministry' hides.

Eulogia normally means a blessing, a good word spoken over someone, and it gives English 'eulogy'. In 9:5-6 it means the gift itself: Paul wants the money ready as a eulogia and not as something squeezed out, then says the one who sows for eulogia will reap for eulogia. Hebrew usage stands behind it, where a berakhah can be a present handed over (Genesis 33:11, 1 Samuel 25:27).

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul urges generous giving as cheerful sowing, assuring God’s provision and resulting thanksgiving to Him.

stories.title: ⚖️ 2 Corinthians 10
summaryBullets: Now by the mildness and gentleness of Christ, I appeal to you — I, Paul, who am humble when face to face with you, but bold when away. (10:1).
I beg you that when I come I may not need to be as bold as I expect toward those who presume that we live according to the flesh. (10:2).
For though we live in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh. (10:3).
The weapons of our warfare are not the weapons of the flesh. Instead, they have divine power to demolish strongholds. (10:4).
We demolish arguments and every presumption set up against the knowledge of God; and we take captive every thought to make it obedient to Christ. (10:5).
And we will be ready to punish every act of disobedience, as soon as your obedience is complete. (10:6).
You are looking at outward appearances. If anyone is confident that he belongs to Christ, he should remind himself that we belong to Christ just as much as he does. (10:7).
For even if I boast somewhat excessively about the authority the Lord gave us for building you up rather than tearing you down, I will not be ashamed. (10:8).
I do not want to seem to be trying to frighten you by my letters. (10:9).
For some say, “His letters are weighty and forceful, but his physical presence is unimpressive, and his speaking is of no account.” (10:10).
Such people should consider that what we are in our letters when absent, we will be in our actions when present. (10:11).

We do not dare to classify or compare ourselves with some who commend themselves. When they measure themselves by themselves and compare themselves with themselves, they show their ignorance. (10:12).
We, however, will not boast beyond our limits, but only within the field of influence that God has assigned to us — a field that reaches even to you. (10:13).
We are not overstepping our bounds, as if we had not come to you. Indeed, we were the first to reach you with the gospel of Christ. (10:14).
Neither do we boast beyond our limits in the labors of others. But we hope that as your faith increases, our area of influence among you will greatly increase as well, (10:15).
so that we can preach the gospel in the regions beyond you. Then we will not be boasting in the work already done in another man’s territory. (10:16).
Rather, “Let him who boasts boast in the Lord.” (10:17).
For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends. (10:18).
crossRefs: Jeremiah 9:23-24: Let him who boasts boast in the Lord.
Ephesians 6:10-17: Armor of God as spiritual weapons.
1 Corinthians 2:3-5: Weakness but Spirit’s power.
Romans 15:20: Paul’s aim to preach where Christ not named.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מָצוֹד (māṣwōd), Greek: ὀχύρωμα (ὀchύrōma, NT), Aramaic: מצודתא (מצודתא)
translationNotes.note: Refers to fortified places; figuratively for entrenched arguments and barriers against God’s knowledge.

Paul appeals in 10:1 by the meekness and epieikeia of Christ. Epieikeia was a legal virtue in Greek: Aristotle defines it in the Nicomachean Ethics 5.10 as the correction of law where the law fails because it has to speak in general terms. It is what a judge shows who has every right to press the letter and does not.

A kanon was a straight rod used for measuring, and from that a fixed standard or an assigned boundary. In 10:13-16 it is the territory God measured out to Paul, which is why he will not build on another man's foundation or take credit for work already done. The same word later gives English 'canon'.

translationNotes.term: His speech is of no account
translationNotes.original: Greek: ὁ λόγος ἐξουθενημένος (ho logos exouthenemenos)
translationNotes.note: Public speaking was a competitive profession in a Greek city, and an audience judged a speaker on voice, bearing and delivery as much as on content; traveling orators drew crowds and charged fees. The complaint quoted in 10:10, that Paul's letters are weighty but his bodily presence is weak, is an attack in that trade's own terms. He answers it with the assignment God measured out to him rather than with a display.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul defends his authority as given by the Lord for building up, contrasting his critics’ self-commendation with boasting only in the Lord.

stories.title: ⚖️ 2 Corinthians 11
summaryBullets: I hope you will put up with a little of my foolishness, but you are already doing that. (11:1).
I am jealous for you with a godly jealousy. For I promised you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ. (11:2).
I am afraid, however, that just as Eve was deceived by the serpent’s cunning, your minds may be led astray from your simple and pure devotion to Christ. (11:3).

For if someone comes and proclaims a Jesus other than the One we proclaimed, or if you receive a different spirit than the One you received, or a different gospel than the one you accepted, you put up with it very easily. (11:4).
I consider myself in no way inferior to those “super-apostles.” (11:5).
Although I am not a polished speaker, I am certainly not lacking in knowledge. We have made this clear to you in every way possible. (11:6).
Was it a sin for me to humble myself in order to exalt you, because I preached the gospel of God to you free of charge? (11:7).
I robbed other churches by accepting their support in order to serve you. (11:8).

And when I was with you and in need, I was not a burden to anyone; for the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my needs. I have refrained from being a burden to you in any way, and I will continue to do so. (11:9).
As surely as the truth of Christ is in me, this boasting of mine will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia. (11:10).
Why? Because I do not love you? God knows I do! (11:11).
But I will keep on doing what I am doing, in order to undercut those who want an opportunity to be regarded as our equals in the things of which they boast. (11:12).
For such men are false apostles, deceitful workers, masquerading as apostles of Christ. (11:13).
And no wonder, for Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light. (11:14).
It is not surprising, then, if his servants masquerade as servants of righteousness. Their end will correspond to their actions. (11:15).
I repeat: Let no one take me for a fool. But if you do, then receive me as a fool, so that I too may boast a little. (11:16).
In this confident boasting of mine, I am not speaking as the Lord would, but as a fool. (11:17).
Since many are boasting according to the flesh, I too will boast. (11:18).
For you gladly put up with fools, since you are so wise. (11:19).
In fact, you even put up with anyone who enslaves you or exploits you or takes advantage of you or exalts himself or strikes you in the face. (11:20).
To my shame I concede that we were too weak for that! Speaking as a fool, however, I can match what anyone else dares to boast about. (11:21).
Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they descendants of Abraham? So am I. (11:22).
Are they servants of Christ? (I am speaking as if I were out of my mind.) I am so much more: in harder labor, in more imprisonments, in worse beatings, in frequent danger of death. (11:23).
Five times I received from the Jews the forty lashes minus one. (11:24).
Three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I was shipwrecked. I spent a night and a day in the open sea. (11:25).

In my frequent journeys, I have been in danger from rivers and from bandits, in danger from my countrymen and from the Gentiles, in danger in the city and in the country, in danger on the sea and among false brothers, (11:26).
in labor and toil and often without sleep, in hunger and thirst and often without food, in cold and exposure. (11:27).
Apart from these external trials, I face daily the pressure of my concern for all the churches. (11:28).
Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is led into sin, and I do not burn with grief? (11:29).
If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness. (11:30).
The God and Father of the Lord Jesus, who is forever worthy of praise, knows that I am not lying. (11:31).
In Damascus, the governor under King Aretas secured the city of the Damascenes in order to arrest me. (11:32).
But I was lowered in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped his grasp. (11:33).
crossRefs: Genesis 3:1-5: Serpent deceives Eve.
Galatians 1:6-9: Another gospel condemned.
Acts 20:29-30: Fierce wolves will not spare the flock.
Matthew 7:15: False prophets in sheep’s clothing.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁלִיחִים גְּדוֹלִים (šəliyḥiym gədwōliym, sense), Greek: τῶν ὑπερλίαν ἀποστόλων (tῶn ὑperlίan ἀpostόlōn, NT), Aramaic: שליחיא רברבין (שליחיא רברבין)
translationNotes.note: Paul’s ironic label for opponents who claimed superior authority or status.

translationNotes.original: Greek: τεσσεράκοντα παρὰ μίαν (tesserakonta para mian)
translationNotes.note: Deuteronomy 25:3 caps a flogging at forty strokes so that the man is not degraded. Jewish practice stopped at thirty-nine so a miscount could not break the limit; the Mishnah, Makkot 3:10, fixes the number as forty less one and divides the strokes, a third on the chest and two thirds on the back. Paul says in 11:24 he took that five times, which is 195 strokes.

A different punishment from the synagogue lashing, and a Roman one. The lictors who walked ahead of a magistrate carried bundled rods, and a beating with them was a standard civic penalty; Acts 16:22-23 shows it done to Paul at Philippi. Inflicting it on a Roman citizen who had not been condemned was illegal, which is the ground of his protest in Acts 16:37, and Cicero had made a public scandal of exactly that in prosecuting Verres in 70 BC.

Opsonion was a soldier's pay, originally the allowance for his rations, and it is the word in 11:8 when Paul says he robbed other churches by taking wages from them in order to serve Corinth. John the Baptist tells soldiers to be content with their opsonia in Luke 3:14, and Romans 6:23 calls death the opsonion sin pays out. Under Augustus a legionary drew 225 denarii a year in three installments, and a denarius was a day's wage for a labourer (Matthew 20:2).

stories.keyTakeaway: Jealous with a godly jealousy, Paul warns that as the serpent deceived Eve, so false apostles proclaiming another Jesus masquerade as servants of righteousness, just as Satan masquerades as an angel of light; speaking as a fool he boasts in greater labors, imprisonments, beatings, a stoning, shipwrecks, dangers, hunger, and daily concern for all the churches, boasting in what shows his weakness.

stories.title: ⚖️ 2 Corinthians 12
summaryBullets: I must go on boasting. Although there is nothing to gain, I will go on to visions and revelations from the Lord. (12:1).
I know a man in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven. Whether it was in the body or out of it I do not know, but God knows. (12:2).
And I know that this man— whether in the body or out of it I do not know, but God knows— (12:3).
was caught up to Paradise. The things he heard were inexpressible, things that man is not permitted to tell. (12:4).
I will boast about such a man, but I will not boast about myself, except in my weaknesses. (12:5).
Even if I wanted to boast, I would not be a fool, because I would be speaking the truth. But I refrain, so no one will credit me with more than he sees in me or hears from me, (12:6).
or because of these surpassingly great revelations. So to keep me from becoming conceited, I was given a thorn in my flesh, a messenger of Satan, to torment me. (12:7).
Three times I pleaded with the Lord to take it away from me. (12:8).

But He said to me, [J]“My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness.”[/J] Therefore I will boast all the more gladly in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest on me. (12:9).
That is why, for the sake of Christ, I delight in weaknesses, in insults, in hardships, in persecutions, in difficulties. For when I am weak, then I am strong. (12:10).
I have become a fool, but you drove me to it. In fact, you should have commended me, since I am in no way inferior to those “super-apostles,” even though I am nothing. (12:11).
The marks of a true apostle — signs, wonders, and miracles — were performed among you with great perseverance. (12:12).
In what way were you inferior to the other churches, except that I was not a burden to you? Forgive me this wrong! (12:13).

See, I am ready to come to you a third time, and I will not be a burden, because I am not seeking your possessions, but you. For children should not have to save up for their parents, but parents for their children. (12:14).
And for the sake of your souls, I will most gladly spend my money and myself. If I love you more, will you love me less? (12:15).
Be that as it may, I was not a burden to you; but crafty as I am, I caught you by trickery. (12:16).
Did I exploit you by anyone I sent you? (12:17).
I urged Titus to visit you, and I sent our brother with him. Did Titus exploit you in any way? Did we not walk in the same Spirit and follow in the same footsteps? (12:18).
Have you been thinking all along that we were making a defense to you? We speak before God in Christ, and all of this, beloved, is to build you up. (12:19).

For I am afraid that when I come, I may not find you as I wish, and you may not find me as you wish. I fear that there may be quarreling, jealousy, rage, rivalry, slander, gossip, arrogance, and disorder. (12:20).

I am afraid that when I come again, my God will humble me before you, and I will be grieved over many who have sinned earlier and have not repented of their acts of impurity, sexual immorality, and debauchery. (12:21).
crossRefs: Ezekiel 1:1: Visions of God.
Acts 14:19: Persecutions endured.
Job 2:7: Satan strikes with affliction.
Deuteronomy 32:36: The Lord vindicates his people when their strength is gone.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שָׁמַיִם הַשְּׁלִישִׁים (shāmayim ha-shlishim, sense), Greek: τρίτου οὐρανοῦ (trítou ouranoû, NT), Aramaic: שמיא תליתאי (šmayyā telītāy)
translationNotes.note: Jewish cosmology often viewed multiple heavens; the third as the dwelling of God.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סִיר בְּבָשָׂר (sîr be-bāśār, sense), Greek: σκόλοψ τῇ σαρκί (skóloops tē sarkí, NT), Aramaic: חוחא בבסרא (ḥūḥā be-besrā)
translationNotes.note: Metaphor for painful affliction; its exact nature unspecified.

A loanword from Persian originally meaning a royal walled garden. Used in the Septuagint for the Garden of Eden. Jesus tells the thief on the cross 'today you will be with Me in Paradise' (Luke 23:43); Paul is caught up into 'the third heaven, which is Paradise' (2 Corinthians 12:2-4); the conqueror is promised access to 'the tree of life in the paradise of God' (Revelation 2:7).
translationNotes.original: Greek: παράδεισος (paradeisos), from Persian for 'walled garden'

translationNotes.term: boasting, and the rules for it
translationNotes.note: Speaking well of yourself was a recognized problem in ancient public speaking, with conventions for doing it acceptably: only under attack, only briefly, and with an apology attached. Paul keeps flagging the whole stretch from 11:1 to 12:13 as folly and says at 12:11 that they forced him into it. What he then lists is the reverse of what any orator would have chosen: floggings, a stoning, shipwrecks, sleepless nights, hunger, and being let down a wall in a basket.

translationNotes.term: what the word thorn actually pictures
translationNotes.original: Greek: σκόλοψ (skolops), a stake or splinter
translationNotes.note: The word means a sharp piece of wood, from a splinter driven under the skin up to a stake, so the picture is of something lodged in the body that will not come out. Paul does not name the condition, and Scripture never identifies it. What he does say is that it was given, that he asked three times for it to go, and that the answer was no (12:7-9). Galatians 4:13-15 mentions a bodily illness that first brought him to Galatia and the readiness of those believers to have torn out their own eyes for him.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul recounts visions, his thorn in the flesh, Christ’s word about grace in weakness, and his selfless ministry despite critics.

stories.title: ⚖️ 2 Corinthians 13
summaryBullets: This is the third time I am coming to you. “Every matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses.” (13:1).
I already warned you the second time I was with you. So now in my absence I warn those who sinned earlier and everyone else: If I return, I will not spare anyone, (13:2).
since you are demanding proof that Christ is speaking through me. He is not weak in dealing with you but is powerful among you. (13:3).
For He was indeed crucified in weakness, yet He lives by God’s power. For we are also weak in Him, yet by God’s power we will live with Him concerning you. (13:4).
Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith; test yourselves. Do you not realize that Jesus Christ is in you — unless you fail the test? (13:5).
And I hope you will realize that we have not failed the test. (13:6).
Now we pray to God that you will not do anything wrong — not that we will appear to have stood the test, but that you will do what is right, even if we appear to have failed. (13:7).
For we cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth. (13:8).
In fact, we rejoice when we are weak but you are strong, and our prayer is for your perfection. (13:9).

This is why I write these things while absent, so that when I am present I will not need to be severe in my use of the authority that the Lord gave me for building you up, not for tearing you down. (13:10).
Finally, brothers, rejoice! Aim for perfect harmony, encourage one another, be of one mind, live in peace. And the God of love and peace will be with you. (13:11).
Greet one another with a holy kiss. (13:12).
All the saints send you greetings. (13:13).
The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all of you. (13:14).

Lamentations 3:40: Let us test and examine our ways.
Galatians 6:4: Each test his own work.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּחָן נַפְשְׁכֶם (bəḥān napəšəkem, sense), Greek: ἑαυτοὺς πειράζετε (ἑautoὺs peirάzete, NT), Aramaic: בחון נפשכון (בחון נפשכון)
translationNotes.note: Call to test and prove authenticity of faith, recognizing Christ’s presence within.

The pair belongs to metal testing. Dokimos is what passed assay, the coin or bar proved to be the metal it claims; adokimos is what failed and is thrown out. Paul uses adokimos three times in three verses at 13:5-7, and the test he tells them to run is on themselves, not on him.

The verb means putting a thing back into working order. It is the word for James and John mending their nets in Matthew 4:21 and for restoring a person caught in a trespass in Galatians 6:1. In 13:11 Paul is not telling the Corinthians to cheer up; he is telling them to be repaired.

An ordinary Greek letter closed with greetings passed to third parties and a one-word farewell, erroso, 'be in health'. Paul keeps the greetings, including the standing instruction to greet one another with a holy kiss, and replaces the health wish with a blessing; 13:14 names grace, love and fellowship together. He signs several letters in his own hand so the ending cannot be forged (Galatians 6:11, 2 Thessalonians 3:17).

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul gives final warnings, urging self-examination and repentance, emphasizing that his authority is for building up, not destroying.

intro:
2 Corinthians was written by Paul the apostle (2 Corinthians 1:1), with Timothy named as co-greeter. The letter was composed in Macedonia (probably from Philippi) in late AD 55 or early AD 56, during Paul's third missionary journey, after Paul had left Ephesus and traveled overland through Troas to meet his messenger Titus, who was returning from Corinth (Acts 20:1-2; 2 Corinthians 2:12-13; 7:5-7). The letter is the fourth (and second surviving) of at least four letters Paul wrote to Corinth: (1) a lost first letter mentioned at 1 Corinthians 5:9; (2) our canonical 1 Corinthians, written from Ephesus in AD 55; (3) a lost "severe letter" written after a painful intermediate visit Paul had made from Ephesus to Corinth (the visit referenced at 2 Corinthians 2:1; 12:14; 13:1, and the severe letter at 2 Corinthians 2:3-4; 7:8-12); and (4) our canonical 2 Corinthians. The intermediate visit and severe letter had been provoked by deepening problems in the Corinthian church and especially by the rise of itinerant teachers Paul calls "false apostles" and "super-apostles" (2 Corinthians 11:5, 13; 12:11) who had been undermining Paul's apostolic authority and credentials. Paul had sent Titus from Ephesus to Corinth with the severe letter and had then traveled himself from Ephesus through Troas to Macedonia, anxiously looking for Titus to bring word of how the Corinthians had received the severe rebuke (2 Corinthians 2:12-13: "When I came to Troas to preach the gospel of Christ, even though a door was opened for me in the Lord, my spirit was not at rest because I did not find my brother Titus there. So I took leave of them and went on to Macedonia"). Titus met Paul in Macedonia with news that the Corinthians had repented (2 Corinthians 7:5-16), prompting Paul to write 2 Corinthians as his response. Paul (originally Saul) was born in Tarsus of Cilicia around AD 5-10 to a Hebrew family of the tribe of Benjamin, educated in Jerusalem under Gamaliel the Pharisee before his conversion on the Damascus road and his apostolic ministry to the Gentiles; he was martyred by beheading in Rome under Nero around AD 66-67 (see the introduction to Romans for the full biographical sketch).

The historical setting is Paul's third missionary journey through Macedonia and Greece. Macedonia was the Roman province in northern Greece (modern northern Greece and parts of North Macedonia, Bulgaria, and Albania), with major cities at Philippi, Thessalonica, and Berea where Paul had established churches during his second missionary journey (Acts 16-17, c. AD 49-50). The Macedonian churches were proving particularly generous in their support of the famine-stricken Jerusalem church, and Paul was traveling through these churches to collect contributions for the relief offering he would carry to Jerusalem (2 Corinthians 8-9 contains the most extended New Testament discussion of Christian giving, holding up the Macedonian believers' sacrificial generosity as a model: "In a severe ordeal of affliction, their abundance of joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity," 2 Corinthians 8:2). Roman emperor Nero (54-68 AD) was now five years into his reign; the early part of Nero's rule was relatively benign under the influence of his tutor Seneca and the praetorian prefect Burrus, with the great fire of Rome and the subsequent persecution of Christians still eight years in the future (AD 64). Corinth itself remained the wealthy, restless, sexually permissive port city described in the introduction to 1 Corinthians; the church there was as urgently in need of pastoral attention as it had been when Paul wrote his earlier letter.

2 Corinthians is the forty-seventh book of the Christian Bible, the eighth book of the New Testament, and the third of Paul's thirteen letters in canonical order. The letter has thirteen chapters. The earliest surviving manuscript is Papyrus 46 (P46, c. AD 175-225), which contains 2 Corinthians on the same Pauline codex as the rest of the corpus; other early witnesses are the complete copies in Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (both 4th century AD). 2 Corinthians is the most personal and autobiographical of all of Paul's letters: it contains his famous "sufferings catalogue" (2 Corinthians 11:23-28, listing the beatings, imprisonments, shipwrecks, and other hardships he endured for the gospel), the account of his vision of the third heaven (2 Corinthians 12:1-4), and his "thorn in the flesh" passage with the divine reply "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:7-10). The letter also includes a historical anchor at 2 Corinthians 11:32 with Paul's mention of being lowered in a basket from the wall of Damascus to escape arrest by the ethnarch of King Aretas (Aretas IV, the Nabataean king who reigned 9 BC to AD 40); the same escape is recorded in Acts 9:23-25.
